October heat in Pune: What pregnant women need to know
Pregnant during October heat? An expert explains how rising temperatures can increase dehydration, dizziness and fatigue, and shares essential precautions.
October heat in Pune: What pregnant women need to know
New Delhi: Rising temperatures can increase dehydration, fatigue and heat-related discomfort during pregnancy, making hydration, nutrition and timely medical attention especially important.
October may bring some relief from the monsoon, but rising temperatures in Pune can make the transition uncomfortable, particularly for pregnant women. Pregnancy naturally increases the body’s workload, and hormonal changes, increased blood volume and weight gain can make it harder to tolerate heat. Excessive sweating, dehydration, tiredness, dizziness and swelling may become more noticeable during hotter days. Expecting mothers therefore need to pay attention to fluids, food, rest and outdoor exposure while continuing their regular antenatal care.
Why heat can feel different during pregnancy
Pregnancy increases the body’s metabolic demands, which can make women feel warmer than usual. Heat and humidity can increase sweating and fluid loss, raising the risk of dehydration. Dehydration may contribute to headache, weakness, dizziness and constipation. Prolonged exposure to high temperatures can worsen fatigue and make routine activities more difficult. Women with conditions such as high blood pressure or those at higher risk during pregnancy may need additional precautions.
Staying comfortable and hydrated
• Drink water regularly throughout the day rather than waiting until you feel thirsty.
• Include fluids such as buttermilk, coconut water and fresh soups where appropriate, while avoiding excessive sugary drinks.
• Eat smaller, balanced meals with seasonal fruits and vegetables that provide fluids and essential nutrients.
• Wear loose, lightweight and breathable cotton clothing.
• Plan outdoor activities for cooler parts of the day and avoid prolonged exposure to direct sunlight.
• Rest in a cool, well-ventilated room and avoid strenuous activity during peak heat.
• Never ignore persistent dizziness, weakness or unusual fatigue.
Watch for warning signs
• Severe or persistent headache, dizziness or fainting should not be dismissed as routine pregnancy discomfort.
• Very little or dark-coloured urine may indicate inadequate fluid intake.
• Persistent vomiting or inability to keep fluids down requires medical advice.
• Reduced fetal movements, particularly later in pregnancy, should be reported promptly to the treating doctor.
• Severe abdominal pain, bleeding, breathlessness or other unusual symptoms require immediate medical attention.
• Pregnant women should continue prescribed medicines and antenatal appointments even when managing heat-related discomfort.
October heat does not mean pregnant women need to remain indoors, but it does call for sensible precautions. Regular hydration, nutritious food, adequate rest, comfortable clothing and avoiding excessive heat exposure can help make pregnancy more comfortable. Most importantly, unusual or persistent symptoms should be discussed with the treating obstetrician rather than being attributed only to the weather.
Written by Dr Swati Ajit Gaikwad, Consultant – Obstetrician and Gynecologist, Motherhood Hospital, Kharadi, Pune.
